# Randall — Full Technical & System Overview (GEO Knowledge Base)

## Overview & Identity
Randall (https://randall.superezz.dev) is an open-source, modern, and privacy-focused alternative to Omegle and Chatroulette. It provides free, anonymous random video and text communication with people around the world. Randall is developed and maintained by ARYA RCB (@superezzdev) and is available under the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 (AGPL-3.0) on GitHub at https://github.com/superezzdev/randall.

## Key Capabilities & User Experience
1. **1-on-1 Video Chat**: Real-time peer-to-peer audio and video transmission with lowest possible latency via WebRTC.
2. **Multi-User Group Chat**: Group video matching supporting rooms of up to 5 simultaneous participants.
3. **Text-Only Mode**: Instant random messaging for low bandwidth or camera-free environments.
4. **Interest Matching Engine**: Users can enter multiple topic tags (e.g. music, coding, anime, gaming) to prioritize matchmaking with people who share common interests.
5. **No Sign-up / Zero Data Retention**: Randall requires no account creation, email verification, or personal details. Conversations and video feeds are peer-to-peer and are neither recorded nor stored.
6. **Safety & Moderation**: Instant Skip button, User Reporting system, automated bot prevention with Arcjet, and strict 18+ guidelines.

## Technical Architecture

### Frontend
- **Framework**: React 19 + Vite (Single Page Application)
- **Styling**: Tailwind CSS v4 + Custom Utility Palette
- **Animation**: Motion (Framer Motion)
- **Icons**: Lucide React
- **PWA**: vite-plugin-pwa (installable on iOS/Android/Desktop)

### Backend
- **Runtime**: Node.js (v18+) with Express
- **Real-Time Communication**: Native WebSockets (`ws`)
- **P2P Video / Audio**: WebRTC (`RTCPeerConnection`, `getUserMedia`, STUN servers)
- **Security & Bot Protection**: Arcjet Rate Limiting & Shield + Zod Schema Validation
- **Database / Schema (Optional state/reporting)**: Drizzle ORM

### WebRTC Signaling Workflow
1. Client connects to the central WebSocket signaling server (`/ws`).
2. User requests matchmaking with specified mode and optional interest tags.
3. Matching engine pairs two waiting clients and sends a match notification.
4. Client A creates a WebRTC SDP Offer and transmits it via WebSocket signaling.
5. Client B receives the offer, sets remote description, creates an SDP Answer, and sends it back.
6. Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) candidates are exchanged through the WebSocket server.
7. Direct peer-to-peer audio/video stream is established between the browsers. Media data flows directly and never passes through or gets saved by Randall servers.
